rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary countable ones may be repeated or combined as parts of a whole; an individual's distinctness is likewise only relative and possible peers remain conceivable.
rows.anchor: şahsî vâhid de bunlardan biri veya birkaçı ile adede dâhil olabilir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A true unique one has no peer; worldly examples such as earth, moon, and sun are one only in limited respects.
rows.anchor: denilir ki bizim “tek”, “biricik”, “yegâne” dediğimizdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative uniqueness of creatures lets their many values converge as signs of the divine oneness, which consciousness apprehends beyond multiplicity and number.
rows.anchor: ferdde birçok kıymetler toplanıp birleşerek vech-i Hakk’ın birliğine bir âyet olurlar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awareness of the true unique One discloses the secrets of divine remembrance, the return of affairs to God, and God's command as a single flash.
rows.anchor: وَمَآ أَمْرُنَآ إِلَّا وَٰحِدَةٌۭ كَلَمْحٍۭ بِٱلْبَصَرِ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the true sense of ahad, all multiplicity and value are absorbed in God's eternal existence, and even positing a second is contradictory.
rows.anchor: o tek vâhid duygusu, hakīkī ferd duygusudur, ehad duygusudur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Negating ahad negates everything; the phrase ahad conveys universal negation, as lā ahada means that nothing exists.
rows.anchor: ehad nefyde umum ifade eder” denilmekle de bu mâna anlatılmıştır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God merely wahid cannot express ahad unless one means the fully real, peerless oneness that negates everything besides Him.
rows.anchor: cemî‘-i mâ‘adâyı nefyeden tam mânasıyla teklik

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib defines wahdat as individuation and wahid, strictly speaking, as something with no parts, though the word is used for any numbered existent.
rows.anchor: Râgıb da şöyle demiştir: “‘Vahdet’ infiraddır, ‘vâhid’ dahi hakikatte asla cüz’ü olmayan şeydir

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib says wahid is a homonym used in six senses, including unity of genus or species, connection, lack of a peer, indivisibility, and an originating unit.
rows.anchor: ‘vâhid’ lafz-ı müşterektir, altı vech üzere isti‘mâl olunur

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib distinguishes God's wahid from ordinary uses: God cannot be divided or multiplied, while others may also be called wahid; only God is called ahad.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ’nın vasfı olduğunda ‘vâhid’in mânasına gelince ne tecezzî ne de tekessür sahih olmayan demektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term wahad means alone and can describe beings other than God, whereas ahad is reserved for God.
rows.anchor: Bâlâda geçtiği üzere bununla Allah’ın gayrı da vasfolunur

rows.speaker: Ebu’l-Bekā
rows.claim: Ebu'l-Baqa distinguishes unity as indivisibility from unity as having no peer in essence, acts, or attributes; only God truly has both.
rows.anchor: ‘Vâhid’in iki mânası vardır: Birisi ‘vahdet’ kendisiyle kāim olandır

rows.speaker: Ebu’l-Bekā
rows.claim: Ebu'l-Baqa outlines unity of essence, attributes, and acts: other existence is effaced before God, perfections derive from Him, and none else truly acts.
rows.anchor: Ve tevhîdin üç mertebesi vardır: Birincisi tevhîd-i zât mertebesidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahadiyya is more complete than wahid: the latter may denote many things, but ahad means the perfect one whose peer is impossible.
rows.anchor: bu bütün mânasıyla bir ve eşi mümkin olmayan tek demek olur

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina explains ahad as God's oneness in every respect, excluding conceptual, essential, material, formal, and sensory composition or multiplicity.
rows.anchor: ‘Ehad’ Allah teâlâ’nın cemî‘-i vücûhtan vâhid olduğuna ve O’nda asla kesret bulunmadığına delâlet eyler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God ahad and wahid does not deny His attributes; it says their plurality does not compose or divide His essence, and divinity cannot be shared.
rows.anchor: maksad âsâr ve ahkâm ifade eden sıfâtı inkâr değil, sıfâtın zâtta kesreti îcâb etmediğini

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina answers that God's knowing His own essence, which causes multiplicities, entails knowing those effects; their ordered plurality follows the essence and does not impair unity.
rows.anchor: zâtını lizâtihî bilmesine kesreti bilmesi de lâzım olur

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina says plurality among necessary concomitants, whether relational or nonrelational, and among negations does not compromise unity; divine names multiply for this reason.
rows.anchor: Zâttan gerek mübâyin ve gerek gayr-i mübâyin levâzımın kesreti vahdete halel vermez

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina holds that positive and negative attributes return to the same divine existence as relations or negations, without real plurality or otherness in the essence.
rows.anchor: Diğer sıfatların bazısında mânen bir izâfet ile bu vücud, bazısında da bir selb ile yine bu vücud olur

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina explains that wahid negates division and partnership, while names such as knowing and first express relations or negations returning to the same Necessary Existent.
rows.anchor: O’na ‘vâhid’ denildiğinde ondan inkısâmın selbi, şerîkin selbi ile yine o vücûdun kendisi kasdolunur

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina argues that the Necessary Existent is pure good and beauty, source of every beauty, and the most perfect knower, known, lover, and beloved.
rows.anchor: Cemâl, selâmet, hayır, müdrik hep mahbûb ve mâşuktur

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina says intellectual perception surpasses sensation, so God's self-knowledge brings the greatest pleasure; embodied people are like the ill person unable to enjoy sweetness.
rows.anchor: hakīkī güzellikleri, hakīkī lezzetleri mütalaa ederek ma‘kūlün ma‘kūle ittisâli

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina identifies each faculty's pleasure with its perfection, the rational soul's with becoming an actual intellectual world, and God as intelligible and beloved whether apprehended or not.
rows.anchor: Nefs-i nâtıkanınki de bilfiil âlem-i aklî olmasıdır. İmdi Vâcibu’l-vücûd zâtında ma‘kuldür

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina describes the first principle as beyond genus, definition, quantity, place, time, motion, peers, opposites, and every actual, imagined, or intellectual division.
rows.anchor: Bir cinste dâhil değil, bir had veya burhan tahtında vukū‘a gelmez, kemmiyetten ve keyfiyetten

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina says God is one because His unique existence admits no sharing and because He is complete in existence, with nothing left to await.
rows.anchor: O tamam olmak için intizar edecek bir şey kalmamış tâmmü’l-vücûd olduğu için vâhiddir

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi divides divine attributes into positive or relational ones and negative ones; creation indicates both kinds, Allah names the positive totality, and ahad the negative totality.
rows.anchor: ‘Allah’ dememiz, sıfât-ı izâfiyenin mecâmi‘ine delâlet eyler, ‘ehad’ dememiz de sıfât-ı selbiyenin mecâmi‘ine delâlet eyler

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi says Allah merits worship through independent creation, which requires complete power, effective will, and knowledge of all things; these are the positive attributes gathered in the name Allah.
rows.anchor: Râzî tefsîrinde der ki: “Allah teâlâ’nın sıfâtı ya izâfiye (sübûtiye) veya selbiyedir

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi argues that every composite depends on other-than-itself parts and is therefore contingent, impossible for the necessary origin of the cosmos; ahad negates composition and entails transcendence.
rows.anchor: Her mürekkeb olan gayrısına muhtaçtır

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi infers that an ahad God cannot occupy space, be in a direction, indwell or serve as a locus, or undergo change, since each implies division or relation to another.
rows.anchor: Ehad olunca da mütehayyiz olmaması vâcib olur. Çünkü her mütehayyizin sağı soluna mugāyirdir

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi says ahadiyya entails wahdaniyya: two necessary beings would share necessity yet differ in determination, making each composite.
rows.anchor: iki vâcibu’l-vücûd farzolunsa vücubda iştirak etmiş, ta‘ayyünde temâyüz eylemiş olurlardı

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi answers the puzzle that oneness plus an entity would make three: unity belongs to the entity itself, rather than forming an aggregate of entity and unity.
rows.anchor: Ehadiyet o hakikate aittir, ehad diye hükmolunan zât o hakikatin kendisidir

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi concludes that Allah names the essence possessing every positive and negative perfection, while ahad negates parts and partners; together they affirm unity of essence with all attributes.
rows.anchor: Allah ism-i celâli, hakikatte en güzel sıfatların sübûtî ve selbî hepsinin sâhibi olan Hak teâlâ’nın ism-i zâtı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To know God's unity amid created multiplicity, one must consider attributes relating Him to His works; a bare, attribute-free essence discloses no perfection or entitlement to praise.
rows.anchor: sıfatsız olarak sadece o diye mülâhaza olunan zât medlûlünde vasıf demek olan bir kemâl

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divinity gathers every positive and negative perfection, and that exclusive perfection implies God's essential unity and excludes partners.
rows.anchor: ulûhiyet, mâbudluk her hamd ü medhe istihkākı ifade eden sübûtî ve selbî nâmütenâhî kemâl sıfatlarının

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name Allah denotes the perfect Necessary Existent bearing divinity, and divinity gathers existence, knowledge, power, creation, and lordship as positive attributes.
rows.anchor: Allah, kemâl sıfatlarının hepsini câmi‘Vâcibu’l-vücûd’un zâtının ismidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name Allah also implies negative attributes, since perfection requires negating defects; ahad makes this implication explicit and the following verses explain its negations.
rows.anchor: ehadiyet tecezzîyi, ta‘addüdü, şirki nefyeden bir sıfat-ı selbiyedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi and Ibn Sina maintain that plurality of divine names and attributes does not divide the essence; attributes are relations and ascriptions returning to one existence, against Christian claims.
rows.anchor: İbn Sînâ gibi o da sıfâtın tegayyürü, zâtın hakikatinde ayrı ayrı birer vücud teşkil edecek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Philosophers, Sufis, and some theologians call attributes identical with essence; Elmalılı cautions that strict identity is imprecise because attributes are relations or negations.
rows.anchor: Hukemâ ve sûfiyye ve bir kısım mütekellimîn “hüve hüvesine aynı” demişler diye meşhurdur

rows.speaker: Eş‘arî
rows.claim: Ashari says attributes are neither identical with nor other than God, since they subsist in the essence and thus do not make two entities; Elmalılı calls this safer.
rows.anchor: Eş‘arî “lâ hüve ve lâ gayruh = ne aynı ne de gayrı” demiştir ki sıfat, zât ile kāim olduğundan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some theologians distinguish attribute and essence in concept and therefore call the attribute other, but Elmalılı warns this can suggest a second being.
rows.anchor: bir kısım mütekellimîn de mefhumda temâyüzü gözeterek sıfat denilen zât denilenin aynı olamayacağını

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All Muslim schools agree that plurality of attributes, like plurality of acts, does not imply division or multiplicity in God's essence.
rows.anchor: hepsi de zâtta kesret olmadığından fiilin kesreti gibi sıfatın

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is not a composite formed from essential attributes; rather, attributes depend on the essence, whose being and attributes are necessary in themselves.
rows.anchor: O’nun zâtı sıfâtının muktezâsı değil, sıfâtı zâtının muktezâsıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human concepts of the divine attributes do not construct God's identity; they reveal our dependence on Him and knowledge of His names, rulings, and manifestations.
rows.anchor: ancak O’na olan nisbet ve ihtiyâcâtımızı duymuş ve O’nun tecelliyâtına delâletler edinmiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Fatiha presents Allah as gathering all perfections through Lord, Merciful, Compassionate, and Master of Judgment Day; worship and aid belong to Him, then this account culminates in ahad.
rows.anchor: رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ مَٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ sıfatlarıyla tavsif olunup ibadet ve isti‘âne O’na tahsis edilmiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No created substance, accident, part, whole, particular, or universal is God or a second God; all are created signs and words pointing to Him and expressing dependence on Him.
rows.anchor: ne cevâhiri ne a‘râzı, ne eczâsı ne küllü, ne cüz’iyyâtı ne küllîsi O değildir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying all is He is true only insofar as every creature's existential and intellectual value consists in indicating and returning to Him.
rows.anchor: heme Ô’st = hep O’dur” demek de bir mâna ile doğrudur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No possible world or created totality contains complete perfection: every possible level remains capable of further development, whereas the Necessary Living Sustainer is complete.
rows.anchor: Bütün âlem ne kadar kemâl eserini hâiz olursa olsun merâtib-i imkân nâmütenâhî olduğundan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gnostics continually witness that every thing perishes except God's face, while those who fail to perceive this will perceive it later.
rows.anchor: كُلُّ شَىْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُۥ

rows.speaker: İbn Akīl
rows.claim: Ibn Aqil calls the sound position God's oneness in divinity while affirming His attributes; Elmalılı explains that every perfection gathers in divinity alone in God.
rows.anchor: İbn Akīl şöyle demiş: “Bizce sahih olacak kavil, sıfâtı isbat ile beraber Allah teâlâ’nın ilâhiyetinde vâhid olmasıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some individual divine attributes may also name creatures, but no creature can possess all perfections; worship, love, fear, and reverence belong only to God.
rows.anchor: nâmütenâhî kemâlâtın, bütün celâl ve ikram sıfatlarının en tam mânasıyla hepsinin birden bir mahlukta bulunması muhâldir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basic, widely intelligible tawhid denies partners in divinity, as in the declaration that there is no deity but God and the statement in Baqara.
rows.anchor: Bu mâna sıfâtı teksir ile beraber onların kesretini bir tek ilâhiyet vasfında tevhid ederek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unity in divinity is true and a first condition of faith, yet it does not fully explain ahadiyya, which means perfect oneness in essence, each attribute, and their totality.
rows.anchor: Ekmel mânası gerek zâtında ve gerek sıfâtının her birinde ve gerek mecmû‘u itibariyle ilâhiyette

rows.speaker: İbn Receb
rows.claim: Ibn Rajab says God is one in divinity and lordship with no other deity or lord, and reads the pronoun in either of two grammatical ways as complete oneness.
rows.anchor: Allah sübhânehû ilâhiyetinde ve rubûbiyetinde vâhiddir, O’ndan başka mâbud da yok, rab de yoktur

rows.speaker: İbn Kayyim el-Cevziyye
rows.claim: Ibn Qayyim distinguishes intellectual tawhid of knowledge and belief from volitional tawhid of intention and action.
rows.anchor: İbn Kayyim el-Cevziyye[^113] Medâricü’s-sâlikîn’de[^114] tevhîdin biri marifet ve itikāda, biri de kasd ve amele ait olmak üzere ilmî ve irâdî iki kısmını

rows.speaker: İbn Kayyim el-Cevziyye
rows.claim: Ibn Qayyim says bare affirmation of essence without attributes has no practical value; an attribute-free supposed deity resembles idols unable to see, hear, benefit, or harm.
rows.anchor: İbn Kayyim el-Cevziyye[^113] Medâricü’s-sâlikîn’de[^114] tevhîdin biri marifet ve itikāda, biri de kasd ve amele ait olmak üzere ilmî ve irâdî iki kısmını beyan ederken sıfatsız

rows.speaker: İbn Kayyim el-Cevziyye
rows.claim: Ibn Qayyim says finite people cannot fully praise God's infinite attributes; Fatiha gathers them in praise and details them as divinity, lordship, mercy, and sovereignty.
rows.anchor: bu nâmütenâhî sıfatların hepsi Fâtiha’da hamdde icmâl olunup tafsîli ilâhiyet, rubûbiyet, rahmet ve mülk sıfatlarında

rows.speaker: İbn Kayyim el-Cevziyye
rows.claim: Ibn Qayyim calls those who focus on unity of essence without attributes deniers of the attributes, the Jahmiyya.
rows.anchor: tevhîd-i zât ile uğraşanların hepsini mu‘attıle-i sıfât Cehmiyye diye göstermiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı says Ibn Qayyim does not clarify whether unity means gathering attributes in one attribute, one essence, or unifying essence through attributes.
rows.anchor: bu noktaları tavzih etmemiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı rejects formulations that make unity of essence depend first on unity in one or several attributes; multiple beings can share an attribute, which is what shirk entails.
rows.anchor: Vâhid, ehad sıfatlardan evvel zâtın sıfatıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Polytheists likewise unite multiple beings through a shared kind or species of divinity; this does not make their essences one.
rows.anchor: Müşriklerin yaptığı da müte‘addid zevâtı ilâhiyet vasfında

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı describes the Trinity as dividing divine substance among Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, then reuniting three persons and gods through shared substance and divinity; ahad rejects every such suggestion of shirk.
rows.anchor: üç uknûm, yani Eb, İbn, Rûhu’l-kudüs üç zât hem cevherde hem ilâhiyet vasfında birleşip bir ilâh olmuş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many attributes gathered as attributes in one essence express perfection and uniqueness; multiple essences sharing an attribute is sheer shirk.
rows.anchor: Zâtullah’ta sıfâtın ta‘addüdüne kāil olmaktan şirk lâzım gelmez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no deity besides God's single essence; divinity belongs exclusively to His essence, meaning the attribute is restricted to Him rather than His essence being restricted to one attribute.
rows.anchor: Lâ ilâhe illallah = Allah’tan başka ilâh yok” demek zâtı bir tek olan Allah’tan başka ilâhiyet ile muttasıf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Aqil's intent is that divinity belongs to God's essence, though his wording may imply other attributes are not exclusive; Ibn Qayyim and Ibn Rajab therefore specify lordship, and Ibn Qayyim sovereignty.
rows.anchor: İbn Kayyim ve İbn Receb ve emsâli rubûbiyet sıfatını da tasrîhe lüzum görmüşlerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone is unique in every exclusive divine name and attribute, including the Merciful, Holy, All-Knowing of unseen and seen, Almighty, and Creator; shared names are stripped of creaturely deficiency.
rows.anchor: Doğrusu Allah teâlâ’nın esmâ-i hüsnâsında başkasına ıtlâkı câiz olmayan esmâ ve sıfât Allah, ilâh, rab isimlerine

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine names and attributes signify sacred realities beyond their ordinary lexical meanings; even apparently anthropomorphic attributes must be read through the decisive rule that nothing resembles God.
rows.anchor: murad olunarak birer hakīkat-i şer‘iye olmak üzere ıtlak edildiği de

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is one not only in divinity and lordship but in every name and attribute; apparently anthropomorphic attributes such as establishing Himself over the Throne require interpretation in light of transcendence.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ sade ilâhiyet ve rubûbiyet sıfatlarında değil, sıfât ve esmâsının her birinde de vâhiddir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine names refer to the essence of highest perfection beyond all finite concepts, rather than to concepts that can be contained in human minds; the highest is more than merely absolute perfection.
rows.anchor: kemâl-i a‘lâ birtakımlarının zannettiği gibi kemâl-i mutlak da değildir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even the totality of all actual and imagined created perfections falls short of the highest, since contingent beings remain dependent and capable of further perfection.
rows.anchor: Kemâl-i a‘lâ bunları bir taraftan yaratıp bir taraftan yok edip duran ve ezel ü ebedde

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God's self-sufficient eternal essence creates and destroys all existence; no finite description or concept can encompass Him, who is beyond human forms and limits.
rows.anchor: O bizim mahsüsât veya ma‘kūlâtımızla çizdiğimiz suretlerin, hadlerin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine names do not define or analyze God's essence; they analyze our relations to Him and point beyond temporal concepts to His perfection.
rows.anchor: Esmâ-i ilâhiye bize O’nun kendisini tahlil ile O’na bir had tâyin ettirecek mefhumları ifade için değil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To understand divine knowledge, begin with finite human knowledge and extrapolate to God's eternal, complete knowledge of everything seen, unseen, past, and future; God encompasses us beyond our knowledge.
rows.anchor: her şeyi olduğu ve olacağı gibi hiç eksiksiz muhît ve binâen‘aleyh gāib ve şâhid bütün kemâlâtı câmi‘kadîm ilm-i ekmel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says God has seventy thousand veils and that unveiling the splendor of His face would burn all eyesight; this portrays multiplicities as absorbed before Him.
rows.anchor: Allah’ın yetmiş bin hicâbı vardır, açıverse onun sübühât-ı vechi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sensing this absorption of multiplicity is sensing God as the Conquering One and recognizing that all beauty and perfection exist fully in Him alone.
rows.anchor: Bunu sezmek O’nun Vâhid-i Kahhâr sıfatını sezmektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every divine name points to unity in essence through all positive and negative perfections; plurality appears only in the modes by which creatures receive and signify that guidance.
rows.anchor: esmâ-i ilâhiyenin her biri de bütün selbî ve sübûtî celâl ve ikram sıfatlarıyla zâtındaki birliğine delâlette birdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since divinity gathers the relations and perfections, oneness in divinity entails complete oneness in essence, lordship, sovereignty, knowledge, power, and every attribute.
rows.anchor: zât ve sıfât ve esmâ, cemî‘-i vücûhdan vahdet-i kâmileyi istilzam eylediği

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Belief in unity of divinity is required for faith; merely knowing that God is one in essence, existence, or lordship without affirming divinity does not fulfill tawhid.
rows.anchor: Yalnız zâtında birdir veya vücûdunda birdir, rubûbiyetinde birdir, diye marifet imana kāfi gelmez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Claiming that God is one in divinity but not one in His essence implies shirk in both essence and divinity.
rows.anchor: Allah zâtında bir olmayarak ilâhiyetinde birdir” demek de zâtında ve ilâhiyetinde
